clue.text: Arrears of salary?

blocks.note: surface reading: money owed and overdue, as when wages have not been paid
setter's reading: wages handed over later than they were due, a settlement put off to a future date

explanation.surface: An employee chases pay that the firm has failed to hand over on time.
explanation.walkthrough: Arrears usually suggests a debt, but here the salary is simply paid late, which is the usual phrase for postponed settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: Money that is owed but handed over later than its due date is settlement postponed, which is what arrears of wages amount to.

clue.text: Speak in round terms

blocks.note: surface reading: talk vaguely or in approximate, rounded-off figures
setter's reading: give a description whose shape is literally round, tracing a ring with a compass or pencil

explanation.walkthrough: 'Describe' in geometry means to draw a figure, so describing a round figure is drawing one, not talking about it.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry to describe a figure is to draw it, so tracing out a ring is the punning sense of speaking roundly.

clue.text: Advice on making coffee?

blocks.note: surface reading: a helpful hint, as in a household tip
setter's reading: the word for a hint pairs with the paper through which brewed coffee drips, naming the end of a cigarette

explanation.walkthrough: A tip is advice, and filter coffee is made through paper, so a tip about filtering is literally the cigarette end.
explanation.definitionFit: The cigarette end with a filtering plug splits into words meaning a coffee strainer and a helpful hint.

clue.text: Mistakenly measure article left out - start again

indicators.note: something done mistakenly comes out wrong, so the word's letters end up in the wrong order
what is left out is dropped from the word before anything else happens

blocks.note: taken as written
the indefinite article, here removed

explanation.surface: A careless builder gets a measurement wrong, has to discard a piece, and begin the job over.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to take up again after an interruption, which is starting once more from where one stopped.

clue.text: Cheese produced over here?

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned over means read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: made is a synonym of produced

explanation.surface: A shopper asks whether a cheese is a local product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here?' adds the surface question of whether the cheese is home-made; it carries no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is the round Dutch variety with a red wax rind, named after its town of origin.

clue.text: Increase effect of medication given to patient, perhaps - a familiar drug

indicators.note: perhaps signals the words are only one possible arrangement of the letters, to be reshuffled

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the street name for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A doctor boosts a treatment by giving a patient an extra, well-known drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medication' looks like part of the wordplay but belongs to the definition; 'given' only joins the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: In pharmacology to potentiate is to make a drug act more strongly, often by combining it with another substance.

clue.text: King is involved in story about adherents of royal house

indicators.note: being involved in something places it inside, among its parts
about here means moved around, so the word's letters are shifted into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of story rearranged
K is the chess abbreviation for king
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monarch features in a tale about the supporters of a dynasty.
explanation.walkthrough: K and IS sit together after the third letter of the rearranged story.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkists supported the House of York in the fifteenth-century Wars of the Roses against the Lancastrians.

clue.text: Unsophisticated sort of mineral water brought up

indicators.note: in a down entry, brought up means the word climbs from the bottom, read backwards

blocks.note: naive means unsophisticated

explanation.surface: A rustic type of spring water raised from the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Evian is a well-known French brand of bottled spring water from the shores of Lake Geneva.

clue.text: Notes first issued in France over 200 years ago?

definitions.text: Notes first issued in France over 200 years ago?

blocks.note: surface reading: banknotes put into circulation, a currency launch
setter's reading: musical notes first performed in 1792, the Revolutionary song that became the national anthem

explanation.walkthrough: Notes looks like money, but they are musical notes: the French anthem was written in 1792.
explanation.definitionFit: The French national anthem was composed in 1792 and named after volunteers from Marseille who sang it marching on Paris.

clue.text: In which less may be required to secure article?

definitions.text: In which less may be required to secure article?

blocks.note: surface reading: a smaller payment is needed, as at discount events
setter's reading: also the word for less wrapped round the article A, with the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Bargain hunters pay a reduced price to get hold of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: At discount events you pay less for an item; there is also a nod to the letters of less holding an article.
explanation.definitionFit: Shop events where goods are offered at reduced prices let buyers acquire items for a smaller outlay.

clue.text: Thumbing a free lift to get to Paradise?

indicators.note: thumbing through pages flicks them about, so the words that follow are riffled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hitchhiker hopes for a ride to some idyllic destination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thumbing a lift' is hitchhiking in the surface; cryptically thumbing riffles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is one picture of existence after death, so the question mark marks it as an example.

clue.text: Mishear, perhaps, failing to recognise a place in France

indicators.note: perhaps marks the word as just one arrangement of its letters, open to reshuffling
failing to recognise something leaves it unacknowledged, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
the letter to drop

explanation.surface: A traveller mishears a French town's name and fails to recognise it.
explanation.walkthrough: The a after 'recognise' is both the letter dropped and the start of the definition's surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheims, also spelt Reims, is a cathedral city in Champagne, northeast France.

clue.text: Popular American soldiers sent over to Northern Ireland put on a badge

definitions.note: insignia is strictly plural, but is commonly used for a single badge

indicators.note: something sent over is flipped across, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
GIs are US soldiers
NI is the abbreviation for Northern Ireland
taken as written

explanation.surface: Well-liked US troops posted to Ulster pin on an emblem.
explanation.walkthrough: GI is the standard nickname for an American soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Insignia are the distinguishing emblems of rank or office, so a single emblem worn on a uniform fits.

clue.text: For relaxation, recline on a luxury ship

indicators.note: relaxation loosens things, so the following letters are loosened from their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers lounge on deck aboard a grand vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A large passenger vessel built for long voyages, famously opulent in the age of the great transatlantic crossings.

clue.text: Mammal hard to find in English city

blocks.note: a bat is a flying mammal
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A creature is difficult to spot in a certain English town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a Somerset city famous for its Roman spa.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath is a city in Somerset, south-west England, known for Roman baths and Georgian terraces.

clue.text: Texts used in reading lessons?

blocks.note: surface reading: classes in which children learn to read
setter's reading: the passages from holy writ read aloud as lessons at a church service

explanation.walkthrough: In church, a lesson is a passage from the Bible read out during the service, so these are not schoolbooks.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacred writings such as the Bible supply the passages, called lessons, that are read during church services.

clue.text: Take another close look at net prices, maybe

indicators.note: maybe marks these letters as only one possible arrangement, inviting a reshuffle

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An auditor scrutinises the after-tax figures a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: To examine something again carefully is the plain sense of the verb with its repeating prefix.

clue.text: Teach mob about ritual sacrifice

indicators.note: about here means turned round and round, so the letters are moved into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lectures a crowd on ancient religious killing.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece a hecatomb was a great public offering, originally of a hundred oxen, to the gods.

clue.text: Carpets pal for upsetting best-laid schemes?

definitions.note: a figurative example, from the idiom about upsetting plans

indicators.note: upsetting knocks things over, leaving these letters tumbled into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells off a friend for ruining carefully made plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To upset the apple cart' is an idiom for spoiling plans, so 'upsetting' doubles as a nod to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Carefully laid plans are figuratively the barrows of fruit that the idiom says one can upset and spill.

clue.text: Coat length seen in South of France

blocks.note: first meaning: a garment hemline reaching to mid-calf
second meaning: the French name for the southern region of the country

explanation.surface: A fashion note on hemlines worn on the Riviera.
explanation.definitionFit: A mid-calf hem is a fashion term, and the French call their southern region by the same word meaning noon.

clue.text: TV equipment arrived before artist

blocks.note: came means arrived
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: The broadcast gear was delivered ahead of the painter's arrival.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Television studios film with this device, which captures the moving pictures broadcast to viewers.

clue.text: Establishes new accommodation for livestock in island

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces within the word for island

blocks.note: IS is the abbreviation for island
N is the abbreviation for new
a stall is a compartment for an animal in a stable

explanation.surface: A farmer sets up fresh animal housing on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: To install someone or something is to settle or set it up in place, so establishes is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Hindu teacher seen by American in London area?

indicators.note: in tells us to place one piece within the other

blocks.note: SW1 is a central London postcode, written here with a letter I for the figure one
AM is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A guru is spotted by a US visitor in a district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: SW1 is the postcode district around Westminster; the figure 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A swami is a Hindu religious teacher or ascetic, the title being a term of respect.

clue.text: Slates frivolous ornamental tuft

indicators.note: frivolous means not serious or settled, so the word's letters play around

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone criticises a decorative fringe as being silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slates' looks like a verb meaning criticises, but it is the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A tassel is a bunch of loose threads knotted at one end, hung as decoration on cushions or curtains.

clue.text: Feature of classical building described in parchment

indicators.note: described in means contained within the outline of the word that follows

blocks.note: the second to fifth letters of the word

explanation.surface: An ancient temple's details are recorded on old vellum.
explanation.definitionFit: Curved spans over openings are a defining element of Roman and other classical architecture.

clue.text: What was his was mine

blocks.note: surface reading: a possessive boast, everything he owned belonged to me
setter's reading: mine is a pit, so what he owned was a colliery

explanation.walkthrough: Mine is a noun, not a pronoun: the man owned a pit, before Britain's collieries were nationalised in 1947.
explanation.definitionFit: The private proprietor of a colliery possessed a mine, so his property literally was a pit.

clue.text: Fragrant resin some of clientele might purchase

indicators.note: some of means only part of the following words is taken

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word and first two of the second

explanation.surface: A shop's customers may buy a perfumed gum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' only completes the shopping picture; the letters lie across the two preceding words.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemi is an aromatic gum from tropical trees, used in varnishes, ointments and perfumery.

clue.text: Keep regalia here

blocks.note: surface reading: an instruction to store royal emblems in this place
setter's reading: keep is a noun, a fortified tower, the stronghold where Scotland's crown jewels are held

explanation.walkthrough: Keep reads as a verb but is a stronghold; the Honours of Scotland, its crown jewels, are displayed in the fortress on the capital's rock.
explanation.definitionFit: The fortress above Scotland's capital houses the Honours of Scotland, the oldest crown jewels in Britain.
